analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.25 an hour in two steps.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill never left committee and died without a floor vote at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $4.75 ninety days after passage, then to $5.25 a year later [S2][S3]. It was introduced in April 1996 by Rep. Jack Quinn, a New York Republican, with 29 cosponsors — 23 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S4]. It was sent to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it stayed [S1][S5]. It never received a committee vote or a vote by the full House before the Congress ended in January 1997 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, who would have seen their hourly pay rise from $4.25 to $4.75 and then to $5.25 — an increase of about 24% over two steps [S2][S3]. Many workers earning slightly above the minimum would also benefit as pay scales adjusted upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour beginning 90 days after enactment, and to $5.25 an hour after one more year [S2][S3].
The increase applies under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law that sets the wage floor for most hourly workers nationwide [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum-wage labor — especially restaurants, retail stores, and other small and large businesses with large hourly workforces — would bear higher payroll costs [S2][S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices or offset through scheduling and staffing decisions.

drawbacks.text: Employers of low-wage workers would face a roughly 24% increase in their minimum labor costs within about two years, which small businesses with thin margins would have to absorb through higher prices, reduced hiring, or reduced hours [S2][S3].
A nationwide wage floor of $5.25 would apply uniformly across regions with very different living costs and wage levels, so the burden would fall hardest on low-wage labor markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: a 24% raise over roughly two years for the lowest-paid workers, paid for by their employers and partly by consumers through prices. The economic research on moderate minimum wage increases generally finds small employment effects, though employers in very low-wage areas would feel the squeeze most. The bill was a clean, simple increase without offsets or carve-outs, so its benefits would have gone directly to paycheck amounts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House education and labor committee, then parked in a subcommittee, and the Congress ended without it ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Quinn introduced the bill on April 17, 1996, with 29 cosponsors — 23 Republicans and 6 Democrats, a bipartisan group led by Republicans [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction [S5].
On May 6, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 104th Congress [S1][S5].
The bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, having never been reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers, who kept paying $4.25 an hour while the bill sat in subcommittee, were better off because it never advanced. Workers who would have received the raise lost the opportunity.

for.name: Rep. Jack Quinn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 29 cosponsors behind it

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out; it was sent to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee on May 6, 1996, and no markup or vote followed

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan but Republican-led — 23 Republicans and 6 Democrats signed on — and it died in a Republican-run committee without a recorded vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of minimum-wage workers; a $5.25 floor would raise their payroll costs directly, and their interest in stopping the bill ran against the wage gains ordinary workers would have received.
Retail employers of hourly workers would bear higher wage costs under the bill; blocking it preserved the $4.25 floor they had been paying.
